note: Proposed, not sealed. Evidence for the staleness question TODO.md lists under Open and docs/seal-staleness-and-quorum.md holds. On 2026-09-01 a willows-grove session (heimdallr seat) read Nestor's live household store at ~/.nestor/keep/ over MCP, read-only, and relayed four sealed pairs as statements about this tree. All four were true when sealed. Three had been overtaken by shipped work, and the fourth was never checked against a running command at all. IMPORTANT LIMIT ON THIS RECORD: the four pair_ids below are NOT in docs/dogfood/nestor.db (checked: 0 rows each) and there is no ~/.nestor/keep in this working tree, so the ids and their quoted text are REPORTED BY that session, twice relayed through the operator, and were not read here. What was read here is the other half of each row — the tree-side fact that overtook it — and each of those carries a citation.

decisions.question: What is the measured evidence that a sealed pair goes stale while still reading as a present-tense fact?
decisions.commitment: Four pairs in one evening, each reported as current, each overtaken. (1) `4988f34f-0393-59b1-9391-1112325e5c84` — 'There is no per-domain verifier policy. Measured: add_pair(status=sealed, verifier=anybody-at-all) is accepted.' The allowlist shipped in v0.10.0 on 2026-08-19 (issue #167): `verifier_policy` table at nestor/sqlite_store.py:238, enforced at nestor/memory.py:659 and :821, `nestor policy` in the CLI. Separately and more to the point, with a keyring installed add_pair raises UnknownVerifierError before any store read or write — measured here across five configurations. (2) `96a65094-8b2c-5bef-8c5a-21ce56c97c84` — 'the instance that signs holds its verifiers' private keys ... browser/client-side signing is deliberately left open.' The client-signing seam is shipped: `_resolve_seal_sig` at nestor/memory.py:393 verifies a caller-supplied signature, `keys add --type ed25519 --public` registers a peer's public half (nestor/cli.py:841), and tests/test_client_signed_seals.py passes 14 tests with a frozen wire contract. (3) `1d20e05b-bace-5eb8-a6ac-9b4511e539b7` — 'Not through the entity recipe — it has only seal. Left open, IDEAS §6.39.' EntityResolver.propose() is at nestor/entity.py:91 and IDEAS.md:115 tags §6.39 'measured, fix shipped'. (4) `ce388d48-18c5-54df-a002-d610efc61913` — '`nestor keys add` prints the public half and calls it the only copy. Left open, IDEAS §6.36.' IDEAS.md:112 tags §6.36 'measured, fix shipped'.
decisions.why: The store had no way to be wrong and was wrong anyway. Every one of those seals recorded something a human had checked, and the signature on each still verifies — nothing was forged, nothing was edited, the ledger is intact. What decayed was not the record but the world it described, and Nestor has no vocabulary for that difference. A reader who trusts the seal correctly, exactly as designed, gets a false statement about the tree. Four instances inside one session, found by an outside seat with read-only access to seven of twenty-four verbs, is a stronger sample than anything currently in bench/ for this particular failure, and it arrived by accident rather than by looking for it.

decisions.question: Is this the same failure as a seal that no longer verifies, and can staleness be inferred from what the store already holds?
decisions.commitment: No to both, and the second is the harder half. A seal whose signature fails is already surfaced — the curator lists it as unverifiable and no serve path will use it. These four verify perfectly. Nor is `created_at` sufficient: three of the four were overtaken by a specific release, and the fourth (pair 4) was never wrong about the tree at the moment it was quoted — it was quoted without running the command it describes, which is a different error wearing the same clothes. So the signal is neither 'old' nor 'invalid', but 'the thing this describes has since moved', and nothing in tm_pairs (id, source_text, source_norm, source_lang, target_text, target_lang, status, verifier, weight, origin, created_at, seal_sig, reason, superseded_by, visibility) records what a pair is ABOUT closely enough to detect it.
decisions.why: Worth stating because the cheap fix is tempting and would not work. An age threshold on seals would flag the whole corpus and teach people to ignore the flag, which is the failure mode docs/accuracy.md already argues against for the threshold itself. `supersede_pair` exists and is the right primitive when somebody KNOWS a pair has been overtaken; what is missing is anything that notices. The one signal actually present in these four cases is that each pair cites a code location or an IDEAS section whose status has since changed — which is a hint about the dogfood corpus specifically, not a general property of a memory of translations.

decisions.question: What is proposed, and what is deliberately not?
decisions.commitment: Nothing is proposed as a fix. This decision records evidence and stops there. Three candidate directions are named so a later decision can pick one up with the frame in place, none of them adopted here: (a) a re-verification duty on the READER — a pair that cites a file path or an IDEAS section is checked against the tree before being quoted, which is what the seat's verification doctrine already asks of an agent and no code enforces; (b) a staleness signal derived from the citation — if a pair's text names IDEAS §6.36 and that section's tag has changed since created_at, flag it, which covers this corpus and nothing else; (c) quorum or expiry as docs/seal-staleness-and-quorum.md sketches. Explicitly not proposed: any automatic unsealing, any age threshold, and any change to is_verified_seal — the four pairs are validly sealed and a mechanism that quietly stopped serving them would be a worse failure than the one being described.
decisions.why: The seat rule is that a gate which fires is an answer, and the equivalent here is that evidence which arrives unlooked-for is worth recording before it is worth solving. Picking a direction now would attach a design to a sample of four from one corpus on one night. There is also a second consumer with a stake in how this is framed: the willows-grove session reports it has made this the standing objection to Article IV of its constitutional draft, on the grounds that its Standing axes carry no time dimension — a claim's standing never decays but the world moves. If that framing is right, the answer is a property of how claims are read rather than of how Nestor stores them, and (a) is the direction. That is an argument to have, not one to foreclose by shipping (b) because it is the easiest to build.
